title: Conversational buffering: cost-aware capacity model PRD
author: Marco Chen
body:
Overview

This PRD describes Conversational Buffering: a cost-aware capacity model and runtime contract for managing short-term conversational state buffering, prioritized request shaping, and dynamic capacity allocation for low-latency chat workloads. The feature targets Redwood Hosted and Dedicated runtimes with the long-term intention to support Private deployments (VPC) via the same control-plane semantics.

Context and motivation

Conversational applications commonly issue many small, high-frequency requests (token-limited exchanges, keep-alive pings, short-system-utterance updates). These requests have tight latency requirements but are costly to serve when treated as full, independent inference calls. Current approaches either: (a) force customers to provision excess Dedicated capacity to maintain latency SLOs for bursty small-requests, or (b) accept higher cost per request on Hosted by not employing batching or buffering.

Conversational Buffering introduces an opt-in runtime capability that: (1) groups small conversational operations into short-lived buffers, (2) provides configurable cost-prioritization tiers and SLAs for buffered vs immediate execution, and (3) exposes a consumption and capacity model so customers can reason about economics (billing), SLOs, and compatibility with existing routing/fallback policies.

Goals

- Reduce per-request cost for small conversational exchanges by 30–60% at equivalent latency SLOs for typical chat workloads.
- Maintain P50 latency within 100ms and P95 within customer-configurable thresholds for 'immediate' tier requests.
- Provide clear billing semantics and capacity accounting so customers can trade cost for eventual consistency in conversational state.
- Integrate with Redwood routing and fallback policies (latency-tiered routing, model-variant fallthrough).

Non-goals

- This PRD does not change model-level fidelity or introduce new quantization schemes.
- Not proposing changes to token billing unit definitions; buffering impacts how work is scheduled and metered but token accounting stays consistent with the billing surface.

Key concepts

- Buffer window: a short time window (configurable 10–500 ms) during which small requests for a given conversation id are coalesced into a single inference operation where possible.
- Priority tiers: immediate, standard-buffered, delayed-buffered. Immediate bypasses buffering; standard-buffered aims to preserve interactive feel; delayed-buffered trades latency for higher batching efficiency.
- Buffer budget: per-tenant and per-route budget controlling how many buffered operations are allowed concurrently.
- Capacity crediting: consumed compute for buffered work is debited from a separate budgeting bucket when configured; unused buffering credits do not expire within a short retention period.

Success metrics (initial targets)

- Hosted: mean cost per small conversational request reduced by 40% for tier 'standard-buffered' in synthetic chat workload.
- Dedicated: equivalent throughput per GPU increases by 20% for small-request dominated workloads when standard-buffering is enabled.
- Customer impact: 90% of beta customers report acceptable UX (no perceived stutter) after tuning buffer window <= 150ms.

User stories

1) As an e-commerce chat product owner, I want the chat runtime to aggregate typing and short clarification updates so my inference costs drop while users see immediate responses for critical messages.
2) As a platform engineer, I want to set different buffering budgets and SLOs per-route so support and billing-sensitive routes keep strict latency while general conversational routes save cost.
3) As a CTO, I want predictable billing and a simulated cost/latency estimator before enabling buffering in production.

Functional requirements

1. API and config surface
   - New per-route configuration flags: buffering.enabled (bool), buffering.window_ms (int), buffering.priority (enum: immediate, standard, delayed), buffering.budget_id (string).
   - Admin CLI / Console support: enable/disable buffering per-tenant, per-route; view buffer queue lengths and budget consumption.

2. Runtime behavior
   - If buffering.enabled and request.size_tokens <= 64 and request.conversation_id present, attempt coalescing within buffering.window_ms.
   - Coalescing semantics: merge prefix tokens and KV cache where safe; preserve per-request metadata and respond with per-request deltas.
   - Immediate-tier requests must not be buffered; standard-tier may be buffered up to tenant buffer budget.

3. Capacity accounting and billing
   - Metering: buffered operation counts as a single inference operation for compute usage when coalesced; per-request token billing is prorated to original requests.
   - Expose buffer_credit usage in telemetry and billing exports.

4. Observability and alerts
   - Real-time metrics: buffer_coalesce_rate, buffer_drain_latency_ms (p50/p95/p99), buffer_reject_rate (budget saturation), buffer_billed_compute_wh.
   - Alerts: buffer_reject_rate > 1% sustained for 5m (pager), buffer_drain_p95 > route.slo.buffered_p95 for 10m (page).

5. Safety and correctness
   - Ensure function/tool-calls and streaming responses are not inappropriately merged. Streaming messages must still be delivered immediately; buffering only applies to non-streamed short requests.
   - Maintain idempotency guarantees and preserve per-request headers/metadata.

Non-functional requirements

- Latency SLOs: immediate-tier P50 <= 100ms, P95 <= 250ms. Standard-buffered P50 <= 120ms, P95 <= 350ms (configurable).
- Throughput: runtime must support 10k concurrent buffered conversations per Dedicated GPU (beta target).
- Consistency: buffer windows must be weakly ordered per-conversation id.

Capacity model and billing examples

We define three accounting units: request_tokens (R), coalesced_ops (C), buffer_credits (B).

Example table (ASCII):

| Scenario                            | Requests | Avg tokens/request | Coalesced ops | Billing model                             | Notes |
|-------------------------------------|----------|--------------------:|--------------:|-------------------------------------------|-------|
| 1: 5 rapid 10-token edits (no buffer)| 5        | 10                 | 5             | 5 * token billing                          | baseline |
| 2: same with standard-buffering     | 5        | 10                 | 1 or 2        | coalesced_ops * model_compute + prorated tokens | cost reduced if coalesced |

Operational examples

- If standard-buffering has window_ms=100 and three small requests arrive at t=0, t=30, t=90 for same conversation_id, runtime will attempt a single inference at t=100 combining the prefix and deltas.
- If immediate-tier request arrives at t=50, it bypasses buffering and is sent immediately; buffered inference still produces a response containing the earlier requests.

Telemetry and console UX

Console must show: per-route buffer window, current buffer queue size, live coalescing rate, cost-savings estimate (approx %), buffer budget remaining. Billing CSV export column additions: buffer_credits_used, coalesced_ops, uncoalesced_small_ops.

Rollout plan

1. Alpha (internal) - 4 weeks: implement runtime coalescing prototype for Hosted dev environment, expose telemetry only.
2. Beta (selected customers) - 8 weeks: per-route config in Console, billing export proof-of-concept, invite 5–10 customers with small-request workloads.
3. GA (public) - 6–8 weeks post-beta: finalize billing contract, full Console UX, Dedicated support, and private deployment docs.

Migration and compatibility

- Default state: buffering.enabled = false. Customers must opt-in per-route.
- Provide a simulator tool in Console allowing customers to replay historical request traces to estimate cost and latency impact.

Risk analysis and mitigations

- Risk: Poor UX due to over-aggressive buffering causing perceived input lag. Mitigation: conservative default window (100 ms), immediate-tier override, per-route SLOs, and simulator.
- Risk: Billing confusion. Mitigation: clear telemetry columns, billing preview exports during beta, and explicit contract language in pricing docs.
- Risk: Incorrect coalescing leading to semantic changes. Mitigation: strict safeguards (no coalescing for streaming, function calls, or requests with interactive tool invocations) and unit tests for merging logic.

Ownership and next steps

- Product owner: Marco Chen.
- Engineering lead: Priya Kapoor (serving-runtime).
- Observability owner: Daniel Ortiz (eng-platform).

Next steps (actionable):
1) Schedule 1-week spike for runtime merge semantics and KV cache compatibility (owner: Priya).
2) Design Console mockups and billing export columns (owner: Product design).
3) Build simulator prototype that replays traces against buffering algorithm (owner: eng-dx).

Appendix: CLI examples (beta)

# enable buffering for route
redwood routes update --route-id chat-support --set buffering.enabled=true --set buffering.window_ms=120 --set buffering.priority=standard

# check buffer budget
redwood buffering budgets get --tenant-id T12345
